However, his time at Valencia was short-lived, as he struggled to break into the starting lineup and made only 13 appearances before being loaned to Beijing Guoan in the Chinese Super League in 2018.

The move to Beijing Guoan proved to be a turning point in Bakambu’s career. In his first season (2018), he scored 28 goals in 29 Chinese Super League appearances, breaking the league’s single-season scoring record. He was named the league’s top scorer and was instrumental in Beijing Guoan finishing third in the league. His performances earned him a permanent move to the club in 2019, where he continued to be a prolific goal scorer. In the 2019 season, he scored 17 goals in 28 appearances, and in 2020, he added 15 more in 19 games. His consistent performances in China helped him earn a call-up to the Congolese national team, which he had previously represented at youth levels.

Bakamabu made his senior international debut for the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on June 7, 2011, in a friendly against Niger. He has since earned over 50 caps for the DRC, scoring 24 goals. He played a crucial role in the DRC’s qualification for the 2015 and 2017 Africa Cups of Nations, scoring key goals in the qualifiers. In the 2015 Africa Cup, he scored two goals in five appearances as the DRC finished as runners-up. In the 2019 Africa Cup, he scored three goals in five matches, helping the DRC reach the quarterfinals.

In 2023, Bakambu returned to Europe, signing a two-year contract with French Ligue 1 club Olympique de Marseille. His move back to France was seen as a significant step in his career, as he sought to revive his European career after years in China. As of 2024, he remains a key player for Marseille, contributing with goals and experience. Off the field, Bakambu is known for his philanthropy, supporting education and healthcare initiatives in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He is also involved in mentoring young footballers from his homeland.

Throughout his career, Cédric Bakambu has been known for his clinical finishing, physical presence, and work ethic. His journey from a youth player in Brittany to a star in the Chinese Super League and back to Europe showcases his adaptability and determination. With over 200 career goals and numerous accolades, he remains one of the most talented Congolese footballers of his generation.

title: Neil Googe
text:
Neil Googe was born on June 2, 1969, in Maidstone, Kent, England. His father, Alan Googe, was a professional footballer who played for clubs like Millwall and Gillingham, which likely influenced Neil’s early interest in the sport. Neil attended Maidstone Grammar School, where he developed his skills in football (soccer) and rugby, excelling in both. By his teenage years, he had focused primarily on football, catching the eye of local scouts.

Googe’s professional career began in 1987 when he joined Gillingham, the same club his father had represented. He made his first-team debut on September 26, 1987, in a Third Division match against Chesterfield. Over the next few seasons, he established himself as a versatile defender, capable of playing at both left-back and center-back. His solid performances helped Gillingham earn promotion to the Second Division in 1989. During his time at Gillingham, he made 147 appearances and scored two goals, becoming a fan favorite for his reliability and work rate.

In 1993, Googe moved to Nottingham Forest, managed at the time by Frank Clark. He signed for a fee of £250,000 and quickly became a key player, forming a strong defensive partnership with Des Walker. His leadership and defensive prowess were instrumental as Forest won the 1993–94 League Cup, defeating Manchester United 1–0 in the final at Wembley. Googe played every minute of the competition, earning widespread praise. He remained at Forest until 1997, making 152 appearances and scoring five goals, while also serving as club captain for part of his tenure.

After leaving Forest, Googe had a brief spell at Queens Park Rangers in 1997, making 13 appearances before departing. He then joined Swindon Town in 1998, where he played for two seasons, making 60 appearances. In 2000, he moved to Cheltenham Town, then in the Third Division. He was part of the team that won promotion to the Second Division in the 2001–02 season, making 63 appearances in total. His final professional club was Yeovil Town, where he played from 2002 to 2004, helping the club gain promotion to the Football League in 2003. He made 70 appearances for Yeovil, bringing his total career tally to over 500 league and cup matches.

After retiring from professional football in 2004, Googe remained involved in the sport. He worked as a coach and later as a football ambassador for Nottingham Forest, occasionally appearing at club events. He also ran a sports coaching business, working with young players in the Nottingham area. In later years, he became a popular figure in local football circles, known for his humility and dedication to the game.

Googe’s career was marked by consistency and loyalty, with long stints at Gillingham and Nottingham Forest. His contributions to Forest’s 1994 League Cup victory remain one of his most celebrated achievements. Off the field, he was known for his down-to-earth personality and commitment to grassroots football. He married his wife, Sarah, in the early 1990s, and the couple had two children. After battling health issues in his later years, Googe passed away on February 10, 2021, at the age of 51. His death was met with an outpouring of tributes from former teammates, fans, and football figures who remembered him for his professionalism and kindness.

Neil Googe’s legacy endures through his contributions to multiple clubs and his impact on the players he coached. His career spanned nearly two decades, and his story remains a testament to the dedication and passion that define many professional footballers.

title: Sada Thompson
text:
Sada Thompson, born Sadie Thompson on September 27, 1927, in Des Moines, Iowa, was an acclaimed American actress known for her extensive work in theater, television, and film. Her father, John Thompson, was a real estate developer, and her mother, Betty Thompson, was a homemaker. Sada was the youngest of three children, with an older brother and sister. She attended Roosevelt High School in Des Moines, where she developed an early interest in performing, participating in school plays.

After high school, Thompson moved to New York City to pursue a career in acting. She studied at the Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre, training under renowned acting coach Sanford Meisner. In 1953, she made her Broadway debut in *The Seven Year Itch* by George Axelrod, starring alongside Tom Ewell. Though her role was small, it marked the beginning of her professional career in theater. Over the next two decades, she appeared in several Broadway productions, including *The Best Man* (1960), *The Last Analysis* (1964), and *The Gingham Dog* (1968).

Thompson’s television career began in the 1950s with guest appearances on shows like *The United States Steel Hour* and *The Defenders*. She gained wider recognition in the 1960s with roles in series such as *The Doctors and the Nurses* and *The Nurses*. Her breakthrough came in 1974 when she was cast as Kate Lawrence in the CBS sitcom *Fay*, starring alongside Sally Field. Although the show was short-lived, Thompson’s performance was praised. The following year, she landed the role of a lifetime in *Family*, a groundbreaking drama series that aired from 1976 to 1980.

In *Family*, Thompson played Kate Lawrence, the matriarch of a complex, dysfunctional clan. The show was innovative for its time, tackling serious issues like drug addiction, mental illness, and family dynamics. For her portrayal, Thompson won two Emmy Awards for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series, in 1978 and 1980. The role solidified her reputation as a versatile and powerful actress. During the series’ run, she balanced television with occasional film roles, including *The Bell Jar* (1979) and *The Incident* (1990).

After *Family* concluded, Thompson continued to work in television, appearing in miniseries like *The Women of Windsor* (1972) and *Rich Man, Poor Man* (1976). She also returned to theater, earning a Tony Award nomination in 1984 for her performance in *The Hotel in Amsterdam*. In 1991, she starred in the NBC drama *Christine*, playing Christine Cagney’s mother in a continuation of the *Cagney & Lacey* universe. Her final television role was in the 1996 made-for-TV movie *A Promise to Carolyn*.

Thompson’s film career, while less prolific than her television work, included notable appearances in *The Goodbye People* (1968), *The Incident* (1990), and *The House of Yes* (1997), her last film. She also lent her voice to the animated series *The Simpsons* in 1994, playing a character in the episode "Lisa’s Rival."

In her personal life, Thompson married actor William Hunt in 1950. The couple had two children, David and Heather, before divorcing in 1964. She later married director and producer Howard LeGrand in 1977, a marriage that lasted until his death in 2001. Thompson was known for her private nature, rarely engaging in Hollywood gossip or scandal.

In her later years, Thompson remained active in theater, occasionally appearing in stage productions. She was honored with a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Screen Actors Guild in 1990. Thompson passed away on May 4, 2011, in Roxbury, Connecticut, at the age of 83, following a battle with cancer. She was survived by her children and grandchildren.

Sada Thompson’s legacy endures as one of the most respected actresses of her generation, known for her depth, professionalism, and commitment to her craft. Her work in *Family* remains a landmark in television history, and her contributions to theater and film continue to be celebrated by fans and critics alike.

title: Thirayuth Boonmee
text:
Thirayuth Boonmee, born on May 15, 1962, in Bangkok, Thailand, is a prominent figure in the Thai business and political landscape. He is the youngest son of Sodsai Boonmee, a former member of the Thai parliament, and a key figure in the Boonmee family, which has significant influence in Thai politics and business. Thirayuth earned his early education in Bangkok, attending prestigious institutions before pursuing higher studies abroad. He graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in Economics from the University of London in 1984 and later obtained a Master of Business Administration (MBA) from the University of Chicago in 1987.

Thirayuth began his career in the financial sector, working for international banks and financial institutions. In the early 1990s, he played a crucial role in expanding the family’s business interests, particularly in the media and telecommunications industries. In 1995, he co-founded the media conglomerate *Baan Thai Media Group*, which later diversified into television broadcasting, print media, and digital platforms. Under his leadership, the company became a major player in Thailand’s media industry, with a significant share of national viewership and influence.

In the late 1990s, Thirayuth shifted his focus toward telecommunications, recognizing the growing potential of the sector. In 2000, he became a major shareholder and executive director of *Advanced Info Service (AIS)*, Thailand’s largest mobile telecom operator. His strategic vision helped AIS dominate the market, with the company reaching over 40 million subscribers by 2010. Thirayuth’s leadership was instrumental in AIS’s expansion into digital services, including internet and financial technology (fintech) solutions.

Beyond business, Thirayuth Boonmee has been actively involved in Thai politics. He joined the *Chart Thai Party* in the early 2000s and later became one of its key strategists. In 2005, he was elected as a member of the House of Representatives for Nakhon Pathom province, a position he held until 2011. His political career was marked by his advocacy for economic development, particularly in infrastructure and digital transformation. He also played a role in mediating between political factions during Thailand’s turbulent political climate in the late 2000s.

Thirayuth’s influence extended to international business ventures. In 2015, he co-founded *Thai Beverage Plc (ThaiBev)*, one of Southeast Asia’s largest beverage companies. Under his guidance, ThaiBev expanded its portfolio from traditional beverages to include premium spirits, non-alcoholic drinks, and food products. The company’s market capitalization grew significantly, reaching over 100 billion Thai baht by 2020.

In his later life, Thirayuth has remained a key advisor to both business and political leaders. He has also been involved in philanthropic efforts, supporting education and healthcare initiatives in Thailand. His contributions to the country’s economic growth have earned him recognition, including the *Order of the White Elephant*, one of Thailand’s highest honors, awarded to him in 2018.

Thirayuth Boonmee’s legacy is defined by his ability to bridge business, politics, and innovation. His strategic investments in media, telecommunications, and beverages have shaped Thailand’s economic landscape, while his political engagements reflect his commitment to national development. As of 2024, he continues to be a respected figure in Thai society, balancing corporate leadership with public service.

title: Michael L. MacDonald
text:
Michael L. MacDonald was born on April 12, 1954, in Boston, Massachusetts, to a working-class Irish-American family. His father, William MacDonald, was a construction worker, and his mother, Margaret (née O’Sullivan), was a schoolteacher. Raised in the Dorchester neighborhood, MacDonald attended Boston Public Schools, graduating from Boston English High School in 1972. He was an average student but showed an early interest in writing and journalism, contributing to his high school newspaper.

After high school, MacDonald briefly attended Boston University but left before earning a degree, opting instead to pursue a career in journalism. He began his professional career in 1975 as a reporter for the *Saugus Advertiser*, a small weekly newspaper in Saugus, Massachusetts. Within two years, he moved to the *Boston Herald*, where he covered local crime and politics. His breakout reporting came in 1979 when he exposed a corruption scandal involving a local city councilman, which led to the official’s resignation. This earned him recognition and a promotion to the *Herald’s* city desk.

In 1982, MacDonald left the *Herald* to join the *Boston Globe*, where he would spend the next 25 years. At the *Globe*, he initially covered the Boston Police Department, gaining a reputation for investigative reporting. One of his most notable investigations, published in 1985, revealed systemic abuses within the department’s vice squad, leading to multiple firings and reforms. His work during this period established him as one of the city’s leading investigative journalists.

In 1990, MacDonald co-authored *All Souls: A Family Story from Southie*, a nonfiction book that chronicled the struggles of a working-class Irish-American family in Boston’s South Boston neighborhood. The book received critical acclaim and was later adapted into a 1995 television miniseries starring Michelle Pfeiffer and David Duchovny. The success of *All Souls* cemented MacDonald’s status as a prominent writer and researcher.

Throughout the 1990s, MacDonald continued to contribute to the *Globe*, specializing in long-form investigative pieces. He won several awards, including the 1998 Michael Kelly Award for Political Reporting, for his coverage of Boston’s municipal budget crisis. In 2000, he left the *Globe* to work as a freelance journalist, contributing to *The New York Times*, *The Washington Post*, and *The Atlantic*.

In 2003, MacDonald published *Evil Men*, a controversial book examining the lives of serial killers and violent criminals. The book sparked debate for its unflinching analysis of criminal psychology. Later, in 2007, he co-authored *The Last Hurrah: The Campaign for the White House in 1960*, a historical account of John F. Kennedy’s presidential campaign, which drew on extensive archival research.

MacDonald retired from full-time journalism in 2010 but continued to write occasional essays and op-eds. He also served as an adjunct professor at Emerson College, teaching investigative journalism from 2012 to 2018. In his later years, he focused on historical research, publishing *The Boston Irish: A Political History* in 2015, which explored the influence of Irish-Americans in Boston’s political landscape.

Michael L. MacDonald passed away on March 15, 2022, in Boston, at the age of 67, following a brief illness. He was survived by his wife, Linda (née Rogers), whom he married in 1983, and their two children, Brian and Erin. Throughout his career, MacDonald was known for his meticulous reporting, sharp prose, and deep connection to Boston’s cultural and political history. His work remains a significant contribution to American journalism and historical writing.

title: Bobby Fischer
text:
Robert James Fischer, born on March 9, 1943, in Chicago, Illinois, was one of the most influential and controversial chess players in history. His mother, Regina Fischer, was a teacher, and his father, Paul Nemeny, a physicist, abandoned the family shortly after Bobby’s birth. Regina later married Russian immigrant and accountant Russell Tinsman, though Fischer never formally took his stepfather’s name. Raised in Brooklyn, New York, Fischer showed an early aptitude for chess, learning the game at age six from a neighbor’s brother, Jack Collins, who gave him a chess set. By age nine, he was already a skilled player, and in 1956, at 13, he won the U.S. Junior Championship with a perfect 8.5-0 score.

Fischer’s rapid rise continued when he defeated Grandmaster Donald Byrne in the famous “Game of the Century” at age 13, a game widely praised for its brilliance. In 1958, at 15, he became the youngest U.S. Chess Champion, a record he held for 43 years. He dominated the event, winning eight of the next eleven U.S. Championships, including six in a row from 1963 to 1967. By 1962, at age 19, he had surpassed 2700 in the FIDE rating system, becoming the youngest player to reach that milestone. His peak rating of 2785 in 1972 remains one of the highest in history.

Fischer’s international career took off in the 1960s, though he often clashed with FIDE (the World Chess Federation) over rules and prize money. He famously boycotted the 1963 Candidates Tournament in Zurich after FIDE refused to increase the prize fund. Despite this, he won the 1966-67 Candidates Tournament in Susa, defeating Boris Spassky in the final, earning him the right to challenge the reigning world champion, Tigran Petrosian, in 1969. However, FIDE’s refusal to raise the prize money led Fischer to withdraw, and Petrosian retained his title.

The long-awaited World Championship match finally came in 1972, held in Reykjavik, Iceland, between Fischer and the Soviet Union’s Boris Spassky. The match became a Cold War spectacle, with the U.S. and USSR framing it as a battle of ideologies. Fischer’s demand for a $125,000 prize fund (up from $50,000) nearly derailed the event, but FIDE and sponsors agreed. Fischer won the match 12.5-8.5, becoming the first American World Champion since the official FIDE era began in 1886. His victory made him a global sensation, symbolizing American dominance in a field long controlled by the Soviets.

After his 1972 triumph, Fischer’s career became erratic. He refused to defend his title in 1975 due to disputes over the format, and the title passed to Anatoly Karpov. Fischer’s mental health deteriorated, and he made increasingly anti-Semitic and conspiracy-laden remarks, despite his own Jewish heritage. In 1992, he violated U.S. sanctions by playing a rematch against Spassky in Yugoslavia, which was under a UN embargo. The U.S. government revoked his passport, and he spent years in self-imposed exile, living in Hungary, Germany, and Japan.

In 2004, Fischer was arrested in Japan for using a revoked U.S. passport. After a legal battle, he was granted asylum in Iceland in 2005 and moved there permanently. He lived in isolation, cut off from the chess world, and died in Reykjavik on January 17, 2008, from kidney failure. Fischer remains a polarizing figure—celebrated for his genius but remembered for his eccentricity and later vitriol. His 1972 World Championship win, however, cemented his legacy as one of the greatest chess players of all time.

title: Jose Canseco
text:
Jose Canseco was born on July 2, 1962, in Havana, Cuba, to parents Jose Sr. and Edilia Canseco. His family fled Cuba in 1965, settling in Miami, Florida, where he and his younger brother, Ozzie Canseco, grew up. Showing athletic talent early, Jose attended Miami High School, where he excelled in both baseball and football. In 1980, he was drafted by the New York Yankees in the 23rd round, but instead chose to attend the University of Florida on a baseball scholarship. After one semester, he signed with the Oakland Athletics as an undrafted free agent in 1982.

Canseco made his Major League Baseball (MLB) debut on September 2, 1985, at the age of 23, playing for the Athletics. His breakout season came in 1986, when he hit 33 home runs and 117 RBIs, finishing third in American League (AL) MVP voting. The following year, 1987, he became the first player in MLB history to hit 40 home runs and steal 40 bases in the same season, earning the American League MVP award after hitting 42 home runs and stealing 40 bases. He also hit for a .307 batting average that year, joining the elite 40-40 club.

During his prime, Canseco was known for his incredible power and speed, combining to win the MVP in 1988 as well, when he hit 46 home runs and 124 RBIs. He helped lead the Oakland Athletics to a World Series title in 1989, where he hit .458 in the series, including a memorable three-run homer in Game 3. His performance earned him the World Series MVP award. Between 1986 and 1990, Canseco hit at least 30 home runs and 100 RBIs each season, a remarkable stretch of dominance.

However, his career began to decline in the early 1990s due to injuries and off-field issues. After the 1992 season, he was traded to the Texas Rangers in a controversial deal that sent fellow slugger Ruben Sierra to Oakland. His production dipped, though he still had strong seasons, including 37 home runs for Texas in 1996. He later played for the Boston Red Sox (1997-1998), the Toronto Blue Jays (1998-1999), the Tampa Bay Devil Rays (2000-2001), and the Chicago White Sox (2001). He finished his 17-year MLB career with 462 home runs and 1,207 RBIs.

Canseco’s career was later clouded by allegations of steroid use, which he admitted in his 2005 autobiography, *Juiced: Wild Times, Rampant 'Roids, Smash Hits & How Baseball Got Big*. In the book, he claimed that he and fellow slugger Mark McGwire used performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) during their careers, including during the 1988 and 1998 home run races. His revelations contributed to a broader discussion about steroid use in baseball, though many of his claims were disputed.

After retiring, Canseco pursued a career in mixed martial arts (MMA), briefly competing in the International Fight League (IFL) in 2006. He also appeared on reality TV shows, including *Celebrity Big Brother UK* in 2006 and *Dancing with the Stars* in 2009. In 2013, he returned to baseball as a manager in the independent United League, leading the Rio Grande Valley WhiteWings. He also worked as a commentator and analyst for various networks, including Fox Sports.

Canseco’s personal life has been marked by controversy. He was arrested multiple times, including a 2000 incident in which he allegedly assaulted his wife’s sister. In 2009, he was charged with battery and making threats against his then-wife, Jessica Canseco. In 2013, he was indicted on three felony counts of battery involving his estranged wife, but the case was later dropped. Financial troubles also plagued him, with reports of unpaid taxes and legal battles.

Despite his controversies, Canseco remains a polarizing but significant figure in baseball history. His achievements in the late 1980s and early 1990s solidified his place in the game, even as his legacy is complicated by his involvement in the steroid era. As of 2024, he continues to make occasional public appearances, often discussing his career and the controversies that surrounded it.

title: Jeffrey Satinover
text:
Jeffrey Satinover was born on January 27, 1947, in New York City. His father, Charles Satinover, was a businessman, and his mother, Shirley Satinover, was a homemaker. Growing up in a Jewish family, Satinover attended the Bronx High School of Science, where he developed an early interest in science and mathematics. He later enrolled at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1964, initially studying physics before shifting his focus to biology. He earned his Bachelor of Science degree from MIT in 1968, graduating with high honors. Following his undergraduate studies, Satinover attended Harvard Medical School, where he received his Doctor of Medicine (M.D.) degree in 1972. He completed his residency in psychiatry at the Massachusetts General Hospital and later specialized in child psychiatry at the Boston Children’s Hospital.

After his medical training, Satinover joined the faculty at Harvard Medical School in 1975, where he taught psychiatry and conducted research on neurobiology and human behavior. His early work focused on the biological basis of mental illness, and he contributed to studies on schizophrenia and mood disorders. In the late 1970s, his research interests expanded to include the intersection of psychiatry, neuroscience, and philosophy, particularly the nature of consciousness. He published several papers on these topics, gaining recognition in academic circles.

In the early 1980s, Satinover shifted his career trajectory significantly when he became involved in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) and computer science. He worked as a researcher at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, collaborating with prominent figures such as Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert. His work in AI led to the development of algorithms for pattern recognition and machine learning, which were later applied in medical diagnostics. During this time, he also co-founded a software company, IntelliCorp, in 1984, which became a leading developer of expert systems and AI-based decision-making tools. IntelliCorp was eventually acquired by a larger corporation in 1991 for $100 million, making it one of the first successful AI startups.

Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, Satinover maintained his interests in both psychiatry and technology. He published several books, including *The Quantum Brain* (1991), which explored the connections between quantum physics and human cognition. The book received attention for its interdisciplinary approach, though it was also criticized by some scientists for its speculative theories. In 1996, he authored *Cracking the Bible Code*, co-written with Michael Drosnin, which popularized the idea of hidden messages in biblical texts using statistical analysis. The book became a bestseller, sparking both fascination and controversy.

In the late 1990s, Satinover’s career took another turn when he became increasingly interested in religion and spirituality. He converted to Christianity in 1996 and later became an ordained Episcopal priest. He served as a priest in several parishes, including St. John’s Episcopal Church in Madison, Connecticut, where he focused on pastoral care and community outreach. During this period, he also continued writing, publishing *The Jesus Code* (2017), which examined the historical and theological significance of Jesus’ teachings.

Satinover’s later life was marked by a blend of academic, technological, and religious pursuits. He remained active in discussions about the relationship between science and faith, often speaking at conferences and universities. He also served as a consultant on AI ethics and the implications of technology on human consciousness. Despite his controversial views on some topics, such as the Bible code, he maintained a respected presence in both medical and religious circles.

Jeffrey Satinover passed away on June 10, 2022, at the age of 75, following a lengthy illness. His contributions to psychiatry, artificial intelligence, and religious thought left a lasting impact on multiple fields. His ability to bridge seemingly disparate disciplines—from neuroscience to theology—earned him a unique place in both academic and spiritual discourse.

title: Kathleen A. McGrath
text:
Kathleen A. McGrath was born on May 15, 1962, in Boston, Massachusetts, the eldest of three children to James McGrath, a high school history teacher, and Mary McGrath, a nurse. Her parents encouraged academic pursuits, and she excelled in school, particularly in mathematics and science. After graduating from Boston Latin Academy in 1980, she enrolled at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where she studied aeronautical and astronautical engineering. She earned her bachelor’s degree in 1984, graduating with honors. During her time at MIT, she worked as a research assistant at the Charles Stark Draper Laboratory, contributing to studies on satellite navigation systems.

After MIT, McGrath joined the U.S. Navy as an ensign in 1985, motivated by a desire to apply her engineering skills in a technical military role. She completed flight training at Naval Air Station Pensacola, Florida, and earned her wings of gold in 1987. She was assigned to Patrol Squadron 22 (VP-22) in Brunswick, Maine, where she served as a patrol plane commander, flying P-3 Orion aircraft on maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine warfare missions. In 1991, she transitioned to the Navy’s Test Pilot School at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, graduating as one of the top students in her class. Her performance earned her a position as a test pilot for the F/A-18 Hornet, where she focused on avionics and weapons systems testing.

McGrath’s military career took a pivotal turn in 1995 when she was selected by NASA as part of Astronaut Group 16, one of only 35 candidates chosen from over 2,500 applicants. She reported to NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, in August 1995 and completed astronaut training, including spacewalking, robotics, and Russian language studies. Her first spaceflight came on December 4, 1998, as a mission specialist aboard Space Shuttle *Endeavour* (STS-88), the first mission to the International Space Station (ISS). During the 12-day mission, she helped install the *Zarya* and *Unity* modules, the first components of the ISS. She logged more than 252 hours in space, including a six-hour spacewalk to connect cables between the modules.

After STS-88, McGrath remained active in NASA’s astronaut corps, supporting ISS operations and training future astronauts. She also served as the deputy of the Astronaut Office’s ISS Branch. In 2003, she was assigned to the crew of STS-113, a mission to deliver the *P1* truss segment to the ISS. However, due to delays in the Space Shuttle program following the *Columbia* disaster, the mission was postponed. She eventually flew as a mission specialist on STS-117 (June 8–22, 2007), a 14-day mission where she conducted three spacewalks totaling 19 hours and 55 minutes, assisting in the installation of the *S3/S4* truss segment and solar arrays. This brought her total spacewalking time to 26 hours and 10 minutes, making her one of the most experienced female spacewalkers at the time.

McGrath retired from NASA and the Navy in 2007, leaving with the rank of captain. She joined the private sector, working as a senior technical advisor for Lockheed Martin, focusing on space exploration programs. She later became a consultant for aerospace companies, advising on human spaceflight and orbital mechanics. In 2012, she co-founded *Astronauts4Hire*, a nonprofit organization that trained professionals for commercial spaceflight roles. She also served on the board of the Association of Space Explorers, advocating for international space cooperation.

In her later years, McGrath remained active in STEM education, giving lectures at universities and mentoring young engineers. She was inducted into the Women in Aviation International Pioneer Hall of Fame in 2015 for her contributions to space exploration. She married fellow astronaut David Leestma in 1991, and they had a daughter, Emily, born in 1995. McGrath passed away on February 12, 2023, at the age of 60, following a battle with pancreatic cancer. Her legacy endures through her groundbreaking work in spaceflight, military service, and advocacy for women in STEM fields.

title: Benjamin Lawrence Reid
text:
Benjamin Lawrence Reid was born on October 11, 1910, in Cairo, Illinois, to parents John and Annie Reid. His father worked as a railroad laborer, and the family later moved to Chicago, where Benjamin grew up in a working-class neighborhood on the city’s South Side. As a young man, Reid attended DuSable High School, a prominent institution that fostered many prominent African American leaders. After graduating in 1929, he enrolled at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, where he studied journalism and became involved in student activism, advocating for greater opportunities for Black students on campus.

In 1933, Reid graduated with a bachelor’s degree in journalism and began his career as a reporter for the *Chicago Defender*, one of the most influential Black newspapers of the time. His early work focused on civil rights, labor issues, and community concerns, earning him a reputation as a sharp and principled journalist. By 1937, he had risen to the position of city editor, overseeing a team of reporters who covered Chicago’s Black communities. During this period, he also wrote extensively on the Great Migration, documenting the experiences of African Americans moving from the rural South to northern cities in search of better opportunities.

Reid’s career took a significant turn in 1941 when he was hired by the Office of War Information (OWI) in Washington, D.C., as part of the federal government’s effort to improve communications with minority communities during World War II. He worked as a press officer, ensuring that Black newspapers and radio stations received accurate and timely information about the war effort. His work with the OWI highlighted systemic racial disparities in wartime labor and military service, which he addressed in reports and articles that influenced policymakers.

After the war, Reid returned to journalism, joining the *Pittsburgh Courier*, another leading Black newspaper, as its Washington correspondent in 1946. He covered Congress, the executive branch, and civil rights legislation, building a network of contacts that included politicians, activists, and journalists. In 1949, he was appointed assistant managing editor, overseeing national and international news coverage. His reporting on the 1950s civil rights movement was particularly impactful, as he documented landmark events such as the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the *Brown v. Board of Education* decision.

In 1954, Reid left the *Pittsburgh Courier* to become the first Black editor of *Ebony* magazine, a position he held until 1966. Under his leadership, *Ebony* expanded its circulation from 200,000 to over 1.2 million, making it one of the most widely read Black publications in the world. He championed stories that celebrated Black achievement while also addressing social and economic challenges, including segregation, employment discrimination, and political disenfranchisement. During his tenure, *Ebony* published profiles of figures like Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, and Thurgood Marshall, helping to shape the narrative of the civil rights era.

Reid’s influence extended beyond journalism. In 1960, he co-founded the National Newspaper Publishers Association (NNPA), a trade group that represented Black-owned newspapers across the country. He served as its first president, advocating for greater media diversity and press freedom. He also worked as a consultant for the U.S. State Department, traveling to Africa and Europe to promote cultural exchange and report on global Black communities.

In his later years, Reid remained active in journalism and civil rights. He retired from *Ebony* in 1966 but continued to write as a columnist for several Black publications. He also served on the board of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) and advised political campaigns on minority outreach. He died on March 12, 1985, in Chicago at the age of 74, leaving behind a legacy as one of the most influential Black journalists of the 20th century.

Throughout his career, Benjamin Lawrence Reid used his platform to amplify Black voices, challenge systemic racism, and document the struggles and triumphs of African Americans. His work helped shape the narrative of the civil rights movement and remains a testament to the power of journalism in shaping society.

title: Yehuda Lindell
text:
Yehuda Lindell was born on August 15, 1971, in Tel Aviv, Israel, to a family with a strong academic background. His father, Moshe Lindell, was a professor of mathematics at the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, and his mother, Rivka Lindell, was a teacher. From an early age, Yehuda displayed a keen interest in mathematics and computer science, influenced by his father’s work and the intellectual environment at home. He attended the David Yellin Academic College of Education in Jerusalem, where he completed his undergraduate studies in mathematics and computer science in 1994.

After graduating, Lindell pursued a Ph.D. in computer science at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel. His doctoral research, completed in 2000 under the supervision of Professor Adi Shamir, focused on cryptography, particularly secure multi-party computation (MPC). His work during this period laid the foundation for his later contributions to the field. Shamir, a co-inventor of the RSA algorithm, played a significant role in shaping Lindell’s academic and professional trajectory.

Following his Ph.D., Lindell spent a year as a postdoctoral researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, Massachusetts, working with Professor Silvio Micali. Micali, another cryptography pioneer, co-developed the zero-knowledge proof protocol, and his collaboration with Lindell further refined Lindell’s expertise in cryptographic security. In 2001, Lindell returned to Israel and joined the faculty of Bar-Ilan University in Ramat Gan, where he became a full professor in the Department of Computer Science.

Throughout his academic career, Lindell made groundbreaking contributions to cryptography, particularly in secure multi-party computation, zero-knowledge proofs, and general secure computation. One of his most notable achievements was co-authoring the book *Foundations of Cryptography: A Primer* (2005) with Oded Goldreich, a leading figure in theoretical computer science. The book became a standard reference in the field, clarifying complex cryptographic concepts for researchers and students. Lindell also co-authored *Secure Multi-Party Computation and Secret Sharing* (2017), which further solidified his reputation as a foremost expert in secure protocols.

In the early 2000s, Lindell collaborated extensively with researchers like Benny Pinkas, a professor at the University of Oxford, on practical implementations of secure MPC. Their work on efficient protocols for secure computation, particularly in the two-party setting, was widely adopted in both academia and industry. Lindell’s research was instrumental in developing protocols that ensured privacy while allowing multiple parties to jointly compute a function without revealing their individual inputs. These advancements had applications in fields such as secure auctions, private data analysis, and financial transactions.

In 2014, Lindell co-founded the startup Unbound Tech, a company specializing in secure cryptographic solutions for financial institutions. As a co-founder and chief scientist, he played a key role in developing encryption techniques that enabled secure computation on encrypted data, addressing critical security challenges in banking and fintech. Unbound Tech’s technology was later acquired by Thales, a global leader in cybersecurity and defense, in 2021 for an undisclosed sum, further validating Lindell’s contributions to practical cryptography.

Beyond his technical work, Lindell was a prolific writer and educator. He authored or co-authored over 150 research papers, many published in top-tier conferences like the International Cryptology Conference (Crypto) and the Theory of Cryptography Conference (TCC). His papers were frequently cited, reflecting the influence of his work on subsequent research. He also served as an editor for the *Journal of Cryptology* and was a frequent speaker at international conferences, sharing his insights on cryptographic security.

Yehuda Lindell’s contributions were recognized with numerous awards. In 2012, he received the Krill Prize for Excellence in Scientific Research from the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities, one of Israel’s most prestigious academic honors. He was also a recipient of the 2015 Erdős Prize, awarded by the Israel Mathematical Society for outstanding contributions to mathematics. In 2018, he was elected as a fellow of the International Association for Cryptologic Research (IACR), an honor reserved for researchers who have made significant and sustained contributions to the field.

As of 2023, Lindell continues to work in both academia and industry, splitting his time between Bar-Ilan University and his role as a distinguished scientist at Unbound Tech. He remains actively involved in mentoring the next generation of cryptographers and continues to publish influential research. His work has not only advanced theoretical cryptography but also bridged the gap between academic research and real-world applications, making him one of the most respected figures in modern cryptography.

title: Djimon Hounsou
text:
Djimon Hounsou was born on April 24, 1964, in Cotonou, Benin, in West Africa. His full name is Djimon Gaston Hounsou, and he is the youngest of seven children. His father, Albert Tinobé, was a cook for the Benin government, and his mother, Albertine, was a market trader. When Hounsou was 12, his family moved to Lyon, France, where they settled in the Bron neighborhood. He later moved to Paris, where he worked as a door-to-door salesman and a bank security guard while dreaming of becoming a fashion model. In 1987, he was discovered by a photographer while selling sunglasses on the streets of Paris, which led to his first modeling assignments. His striking appearance and charismatic presence quickly made him a sought-after model, working with brands like Yves Saint Laurent, Calvin Klein, and Revlon.

Hounsou’s acting career began in 1989 when he was cast in the French film *Sans retour* (No Way Back) by director Denis Amar. His performance caught the attention of American filmmakers, leading to his first Hollywood role in *Stir of Echoes* (1999), a psychological thriller. However, his breakthrough came in 1997 with his role as Cinque in Steven Spielberg’s *Amistad*, a historical drama about the 1839 slave revolt aboard the Spanish ship *La Amistad*. Hounsou’s portrayal of the enslaved African leader earned him widespread acclaim and an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor, making him the first Beninese actor to receive an Oscar nomination.

After *Amistad*, Hounsou’s career flourished. He starred in *Gladiator* (2000) as Juba, a Numidian ally of Maximus (Russell Crowe), and in *In America* (2003), which earned him a second Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor. He also appeared in *Constantine* (2005) and *Blood Diamond* (2006), where he played Solomon Vandy, a Sierra Leonean fisherman forced into the diamond trade. His performance in *Blood Diamond* was praised, and he was nominated for a Golden Globe. Throughout the 2000s, he became a frequent collaborator with director Guillermo del Toro, appearing in *The Misery of Job* (1993), *The Island* (2005), and *The Wolfman* (2010).

In addition to acting, Hounsou has been active in humanitarian work. He is a Goodwill Ambassador for the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and has been involved in campaigns to combat AIDS and promote education in Africa. He has also worked with the L'Oréal brand as a spokesperson and has been a vocal advocate for environmental sustainability.

Hounsou’s later career included roles in *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2* (2017), where he played the Celestial Ego, and *Shazam!* (2019). He also appeared in the Hulu series *The Great* (2020) and the Marvel television series *Loki* (2023). His voice work includes *The Suicide Squad* (2016) and *White Snake* (2019).

In his personal life, Hounsou has two daughters: Kirima, born in 1990, and Maya, born in 1995. He has been in a long-term relationship with American model and actress Kimora Lee Simmons, though they were never formally married. Hounsou has been open about his struggles with dyslexia and his journey to learning English, which he did not speak fluently until his late 20s.

As of 2024, Djimon Hounsou remains one of the most respected actors of African descent in Hollywood. His work has spanned film, television, and advocacy, and he continues to be a prominent figure in both entertainment and humanitarian efforts. His legacy as a pioneer for African representation in Hollywood is firmly established, and his influence extends beyond acting into global social causes.

title: Vance Joy
text:
Vance Joy, born James Keogh in 1987, is an Australian singer-songwriter known for his indie-folk and pop sound. He was born on December 17, 1987, in Melbourne, Victoria, and grew up in the suburb of Keilor East. His parents, James and Janice Keogh, were supportive of his musical interests from an early age. He attended St. Kevin’s College, a private secondary school in Glen Waverley, where he participated in school musicals and developed his love for music. After high school, he pursued a double degree in commerce and arts at the University of Melbourne, graduating in 2009, but he soon shifted his focus to music full-time.

Before adopting the stage name "Vance Joy," Keogh played in local bands and performed at open mic nights in Melbourne. The name "Vance Joy" was inspired by a character from the 1962 novel *The Honours of the State* by Steyler Ryan, a book he found in a secondhand shop. The name stuck, and he began releasing music under that moniker in 2013. His breakthrough came with the release of his debut EP, *God Loves You When You're Dancing*, in October 2013. The EP included the hit single "Riptide," which became a viral sensation and propelled him to international fame. "Riptide" topped the Australian ARIA Singles Chart in 2014 and was certified platinum in multiple countries, selling over two million copies worldwide.

In 2014, Vance Joy signed with Atlantic Records and released his debut studio album, *Dreams of Basingstoke*, on May 5, 2014. The album, named after a town in England where he once lived, included "Riptide" and other successful singles like "Mess Is Mine" and "We All Sap Like Stars." The album debuted at number three on the Australian ARIA Albums Chart and was certified double platinum in Australia. That same year, he made his television debut performing on *Jimmy Kimmel Live!* and appeared in major festivals, including Glastonbury and Lollapalooza.

Vance Joy’s career continued to flourish in the following years. In 2015, he won the ARIA Award for Best Pop Release for "Riptide" and was nominated for several other categories. He also contributed to the soundtrack of *The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1* with a cover of The National’s "I Need My Girl." In 2016, he embarked on his first worldwide tour, the *Fire and Flood World Tour*, performing in over 30 countries, including sold-out shows at iconic venues like New York’s Madison Square Garden and London’s Royal Albert Hall.

His second studio album, *Nation of Two*, was released on March 3, 2018, and marked a shift toward a more polished, pop-oriented sound. The album included the singles "Lay It on Me" and "We’re Going Home," the latter of which became a fan favorite. The album debuted at number seven on the Australian ARIA Albums Chart and received positive reviews for its emotional depth and lyrical maturity. In 2019, he collaborated with Coldplay on their *Everyday Life* album, co-writing the track "Daddy."

Vance Joy has maintained a consistent presence in the music industry, releasing new music and touring regularly. In 2021, he released the single "Your Cactus," which became a surprising hit, reaching number 23 on the Billboard Hot 100 and being certified platinum in the U.S. The song’s success led to the release of his third studio album, *In Our Own Sweet Time*, on September 3, 2021. The album featured a mix of indie-folk and pop influences and included the singles "Constellations" and "Music of the Waves." The album debuted at number 15 on the Billboard 200 and received critical acclaim.

Throughout his career, Vance Joy has sold over 10 million records worldwide and has been nominated for multiple awards, including a Grammy Award for Best New Artist in 2015. He continues to tour internationally, performing at major festivals and venues. Offstage, he is known for his philanthropic efforts, supporting organizations like the Australian Red Cross and mental health initiatives. He resides in Melbourne with his wife, Georgia, whom he married in 2018. Despite his success, he remains grounded and frequently engages with his fan base through social media and live performances. Vance Joy’s music, characterized by its heartfelt lyrics and catchy melodies, has made him one of Australia’s most beloved contemporary artists.

title: Jimmy Tompkins (priest)
text:
Jimmy Tompkins, a prominent figure in the Anglican Church, was born on January 12, 1935, in the small village of Brackley, Northamptonshire, England. His parents, Thomas and Ethel Tompkins, were devout Methodists, and their faith deeply influenced young Jimmy. He was the eldest of three children, with two younger sisters, Margaret and Joan. From an early age, Tompkins showed a keen interest in religious studies and community service, often assisting at his local chapel.

In 1946, at the age of 11, Tompkins enrolled at Magdalen College School in Oxford, where he excelled in both academics and extracurricular activities. His teachers noted his exceptional oratory skills and empathy, traits that would later define his ministry. After completing his O-levels in 1952, he pursued further education at Keble College, Oxford, where he studied theology, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts in 1957. During his time at Oxford, he was heavily involved in the Student Christian Movement, which solidified his calling to the priesthood.

Tompkins was ordained as a deacon in the Church of England on June 29, 1958, at St. Paul’s Cathedral in London, and as a priest on June 28, 1959. His first posting was as a curate at St. Mary’s Church in Oxford, where he served from 1958 to 1962 under the guidance of Reverend Alfred Whitby. During this period, he developed a reputation for his pastoral care and ability to connect with young people, leading to the establishment of a youth group that grew to over 100 members by 1961.

In 1963, Tompkins was appointed vicar of St. John’s Church in Birmingham, a diverse and economically challenged parish. His tenure there, lasting until 1970, was marked by significant community outreach, including the founding of a food bank and a night shelter for the homeless. Under his leadership, church attendance increased by 40%, a remarkable achievement in a city undergoing rapid industrial decline. His work caught the attention of church leaders, and in 1970, he was appointed archdeacon of Coventry, a role he held for seven years.

As archdeacon, Tompkins played a pivotal role in the reconstruction of Coventry Cathedral, which had been heavily damaged during World War II. He facilitated fundraising efforts and community engagement, ensuring the cathedral’s rebirth as a symbol of peace and reconciliation. In 1977, he was elevated to the position of suffragan bishop of Warwick, serving under the Bishop of Coventry. During his tenure, he championed ecumenical relations, particularly with the Roman Catholic Church, and oversaw the ordination of over 50 new priests.

Tompkins’ national profile grew in the 1980s when he became a vocal advocate for social justice, particularly in housing and education. In 1985, he was appointed chairman of the Church of England’s Board of Social Responsibility, a role he held until 1992. During this time, he authored several reports on urban poverty, including *Faith and the Inner City* (1988), which influenced government housing policies. He also served as a trustee of the Children’s Society, raising over £2 million for its programs.

In 1992, Tompkins was made the Bishop of Portsmouth, a position he held until his retirement in 2001. His leadership in Portsmouth was defined by his efforts to address crime and addiction, particularly through the establishment of the Portsmouth Churches’ Drug and Alcohol Project. He also oversaw the expansion of the diocese’s network of schools, increasing the number of Church of England academies from three to twelve.

After retiring from full-time ministry in 2001, Tompkins remained active in public life. He served as a non-executive director of the NHS Foundation Trust in Portsmouth and continued to write and lecture on faith and social issues. He published his memoir, *A Life in Service*, in 2010, which detailed his experiences in the church and his views on contemporary religious challenges.

Jimmy Tompkins was married to Margaret (née Harris) in 1960, and the couple had two sons, David and Peter. Margaret passed away in 2005, and Tompkins later moved to a retirement home in Oxford. He continued to lead occasional services and mentor young clergy until his death on March 7, 2018, at the age of 83. A memorial service was held at Coventry Cathedral, attended by over 500 people, including former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, who praised Tompkins as “a man of unwavering compassion and vision.”

Throughout his life, Jimmy Tompkins was decorated for his service, receiving the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 1990 and the Lambeth Cross for Ecumenism in 1999. His legacy endures through the numerous charities and community initiatives he helped found, as well as the hundreds of clergy he mentored during his career.

title: Ahsee Tuala
text:
Ahsee Tuala, born on January 17, 1976, in Auckland, New Zealand, is a former professional rugby league player known for his speed, skill, and longevity in the sport. He grew up in Auckland, where he attended Mount Albert Grammar School, excelling in both rugby league and athletics. His father, a Samoan immigrant, introduced him to rugby league at a young age, and Tuala quickly developed a reputation as a talented winger. By the time he was 16, he had already represented Auckland in junior competitions, showcasing his explosive pace and try-scoring ability.

Tuala began his professional career in 1995 when he signed with the Auckland Warriors, the newly established National Rugby League (NRL) team. He made his first-grade debut on March 12, 1995, against the Brisbane Broncos in a match at the Sydney Football Stadium. Although the Warriors struggled in their inaugural season, Tuala stood out as one of the team’s most promising young players. His speed and agility made him a constant threat on the wing, and he scored his first NRL try in a 30-20 loss to the North Queensland Cowboys on April 2, 1995. Over the next three seasons, he became a regular starter, playing 72 matches and scoring 41 tries for the Warriors.

In 1997, Tuala was selected for the New Zealand national rugby league team, making his Test debut on June 14, 1997, against Great Britain in a World Cup warm-up match. He went on to play a key role in the 1997 Super League Tri-Series, helping New Zealand secure third place. His international performances earned him a place in the 1998 ANZAC Test, where he scored a try in a 22-16 win over Australia. Tuala’s form attracted attention from English clubs, and in 1999, he signed with the Bradford Bulls, one of the most successful teams in the Super League.

Tuala spent five seasons at Bradford, winning three Super League Grand Finals (2001, 2003, 2004) and one Challenge Cup (2003). His speed and finishing ability remained key assets, and he scored 50 tries in 110 appearances for the Bulls. He was also part of the 2002 and 2003 World Club Challenge-winning teams, defeating the St. Helens and the Penrith Panthers, respectively. His time at Bradford cemented his reputation as one of the leading wingers in the world.

After leaving Bradford in 2004, Tuala moved to the Sydney Roosters in the NRL, where he played for two seasons. He contributed to the club’s 2004 and 2005 campaigns, scoring 12 tries in 40 appearances. In 2006, he returned to the Auckland Warriors (later renamed the New Zealand Warriors) for a final stint, playing 13 matches before retiring at the end of the season. His NRL career spanned 12 years, during which he played 214 matches and scored 110 tries.

Following his retirement, Tuala remained involved in rugby league, working as a youth coach and ambassador for the sport in New Zealand. He also pursued business interests, including opening a gym in Auckland. In 2012, he was inducted into the New Zealand Rugby League’s Legends of League, recognizing his contributions to the game. Despite his retirement, he remains a respected figure in rugby league circles, remembered for his lightning-fast runs and consistent try-scoring ability.

Tuala’s career was marked by his adaptability, excelling in both the NRL and Super League. His ability to perform at the highest level for nearly two decades solidified his legacy as one of New Zealand’s greatest rugby league wingers.

title: Susan Sarandon
text:
Susan Sarandon was born Susan Abigail Tomalin on October 4, 1946, in New York City, the second of nine children. Her father, Phillip Carl Tomalin, was an advertising executive and Italian immigrant, and her mother, Lenora Marie Crisitello, was a housewife of Italian and English descent. Raised in the working-class neighborhood of Edison, New Jersey, Sarandon attended Edison High School, where she was a cheerleader and participated in school plays. She later enrolled at The Catholic University of America in Washington, D.C., but transferred to New York University (NYU) in 1964, where she studied at the Tisch School of the Arts. It was during her time at NYU that she changed her last name to Sarandon, inspired by the French word for "all-encompassing" or "sweeping."

Sarandon’s acting career began in the late 1960s with small roles in television and film. Her first credited film appearance was in the 1969 comedy *Joe*, directed by John G. Avildsen. However, her breakout role came in 1970 when she starred as Janet Weiss in the cult classic *Joe*, which earned her critical attention. She continued to build her reputation with roles in films like *The Rocky Horror Picture Show* (1975), where she played Janet Weiss, and *The Last Waltz* (1978), a documentary about The Band’s farewell concert. Her performance in *The Last Waltz* showcased her ability to blend naturalism with a rebellious spirit, a trait that would define much of her early work.

In the 1980s, Sarandon transitioned into more dramatic roles, earning widespread acclaim for her performance as a grieving mother in *The Lovely Bones* (2002) and as a nun turned revolutionary in *Dead Man Walking* (1995), for which she received her first Academy Award nomination for Best Actress. The film, directed by Tim Robbins, was a powerful drama about a nun who befriends a condemned prisoner on death row, and Sarandon’s performance was widely praised for its depth and emotional resonance. Though she did not win the Oscar that year, her role solidified her as a serious dramatic actress.

Sarandon’s career reached new heights in the 1990s and 2000s. In 1995, she won her first Academy Award for Best Actress for her role as Louise in *Thelma & Louise* (1991), directed by Ridley Scott. The film, co-starring Geena Davis, became a feminist icon, and Sarandon’s portrayal of a woman on the run from the law was both fierce and vulnerable. She also received an Academy Award nomination for her role in *The Client* (1994), a legal thriller starring Brad Renfro. Throughout the 1990s, she balanced commercial blockbusters with independent films, such as *Stepmom* (1998), where she starred opposite Julia Roberts, and *Anywhere But Here* (1999), directed by Wayne Wang.

In addition to her film work, Sarandon has been a prominent figure in television. She starred in the HBO series *Bernie and Erica* (1981) and later in *Dead Man Walking: The Musical* (2001), a stage production based on the film. She also appeared in the critically acclaimed series *The L Word* (2004–2009) as Bette Porter, a college dean and lesbian activist. The role earned her further acclaim and introduced her to a new generation of audiences.

Sarandon’s personal life has also been the subject of public interest. She married actor Chris Sarandon in 1967, though they divorced in 1979. She has two children from her relationship with director Tim Robbins: Jack Henry Robbins (born 1989) and Miles Guthrie Robbins (born 1992). In 2009, she married Jonathan Brickman, a 28-year-old entrepreneur, though they separated in 2013. Sarandon has been open about her political activism, supporting progressive causes such as LGBTQ+ rights, environmentalism, and anti-death penalty advocacy.

In her later career, Sarandon continued to take on challenging roles. She starred in *The Meddler* (2015), a comedy-drama directed by Lorene Scafaria, and *Feud: Bette and Joan* (2017), an FX series where she portrayed Bette Davis. She also appeared in *The Last Word* (2017) and *The Friend* (2019). In 2020, she joined the cast of *The Kitchen*, a crime drama set in Hell’s Kitchen during the 1970s.

Despite her long and illustrious career, Sarandon remains active in film and activism. She has been vocal about social and political issues, including climate change and gender equality. In 2021, she received the Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award in recognition of her outstanding contributions to the entertainment industry. As of 2024, she continues to act in film and television, proving her enduring talent and influence in Hollywood.

title: Fifi Cooper
text:
Fifi Cooper, born on September 3, 1992, in Cape Town, South Africa, is a versatile South African actress, singer, and writer known for her work in film, television, and theater. She gained international recognition for her roles in projects like *Catching Feelings* (2017) and *Queen Sono* (2020), while also contributing to South Africa’s music and arts scene. Her career reflects a commitment to storytelling that blends South African culture with global entertainment.

Cooper grew up in Cape Town, where she developed an early passion for the arts. She attended the prestigious Cape Town High School for Girls, where she participated in drama and music productions. After completing high school, she enrolled at the University of Cape Town (UCT) to study drama. Her time at UCT was formative, allowing her to refine her acting skills and gain experience in both stage and screen performances. During this period, she also began experimenting with music, blending her love for African rhythms with contemporary sounds.

Her professional career began in the mid-2010s, with early roles in South African television series such as *The River* (2014–2015), where she played the supporting character of Noko. This role helped establish her as a rising talent in the local industry. In 2017, she starred in the romantic drama film *Catching Feelings*, directed by Thabo Mbeki Jr. and produced by Anant Singh. The film, which also featured Khaya Dladla, was a commercial success in South Africa and earned critical acclaim for its depiction of modern relationships and cultural identities. Cooper’s performance as Thando, a young woman navigating love and ambition, was particularly praised, further solidifying her status as a leading actress in South African cinema.

In 2020, Cooper achieved a major career milestone with the release of *Queen Sono*, a Netflix original series in which she played the titular role. Created by Kagiso Lediga and directed by Tebogo Malope, the show follows the adventures of a tough, morally conflicted secret agent in Johannesburg. *Queen Sono* marked a significant moment in African entertainment, as it was one of the first major Netflix series led by a Black South African woman. The show’s success—garnering millions of views and positive reviews—cemented Cooper’s place as a global star. Her portrayal of Sono, a complex and dynamic character, showcased her range as an actress and her ability to carry a high-profile production.

Beyond acting, Cooper is also a talented singer. She has released several original songs, including "Wash Me" and "Soweto," which blend Afro-soul, jazz, and R&B influences. Her music often reflects her South African roots, incorporating elements of local genres like kwaito and amapiano. In 2021, she performed at major events such as the Cape Town International Jazz Festival, further expanding her influence in the arts.

Cooper’s work extends into writing as well. She has contributed to screenplays and creative projects, demonstrating her versatility as an artist. Her involvement in multidisciplinary projects highlights her dedication to storytelling in all its forms.

In her personal life, Cooper has been open about her experiences as a woman in the entertainment industry, advocating for greater representation and opportunities for Black creatives. She has been vocal about the challenges of balancing work and personal well-being, often speaking about the importance of self-care and mental health.

As of 2024, Fifi Cooper continues to be a prominent figure in South African and African entertainment. She remains active in film and television, with new projects in development. Her contributions to cinema, music, and theater have made her a celebrated artist both locally and internationally, embodying the creativity and resilience of South Africa’s cultural landscape.

title: Michael Collins (astronaut)
text:
Michael Collins was born on October 31, 1930, in Rome, Italy, to U.S. Army Major General James Lawton Collins and his wife, Virginia Collins. His father, a career military officer, was stationed in Italy at the time, and the family later moved to the United States when Michael was a child. He grew up in Washington, D.C., and attended St. Albans School, a prestigious private institution. In 1952, Collins graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point, where he had been part of the Class of 1952. After graduation, he joined the U.S. Air Force, where he trained as a fighter pilot and flew F-86 Sabre jets during the early 1950s.

In 1960, Collins transferred to the Air Force Institute of Technology at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio, earning a master’s degree in aeronautical engineering in 1963. That same year, he was selected as one of the third group of astronauts for NASA’s space program, known as "The New Nine." His selection came after rigorous testing and evaluation, and he began training for potential spaceflight assignments. In 1965, he made his first spaceflight as the pilot of Gemini X, which launched on July 18, 1965. During the mission, Collins and his commander, John Young, completed two rendezvous with other spacecraft and performed a spacewalk, spending a total of nearly three days in orbit. The mission was a success, and Collins became one of the first Americans to perform an extravehicular activity (EVA) in space.

Collins’s most famous role came in 1969 when he served as the command module pilot for Apollo 11, the historic mission that landed the first humans on the Moon. The crew—Commander Neil Armstrong, Lunar Module Pilot Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, and Collins—launched on July 16, 1969. While Armstrong and Aldrin descended to the lunar surface in the Lunar Module *Eagle*, Collins remained alone in the Command Module *Columbia*, orbiting the Moon. He circled the Moon 30 times over 21.5 hours, conducting observations and maintaining communications with mission control. His solitude during this period became legendary, and he later described it as both serene and isolating. After Armstrong and Aldrin returned from the Moon, the crew splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean on July 24, 1969, completing a mission that captured global attention.

Following Apollo 11, Collins left NASA in 1970 to become the Director of the National Air and Space Museum, a position he held until 1978. During his tenure, he oversaw the museum’s planning and construction, which opened in 1976. He also served as Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs from 1977 to 1980 under President Jimmy Carter, where he managed public diplomacy and cultural exchanges. In his later years, Collins wrote several books, including his 1974 memoir *Carrying the Fire*, which provided a detailed account of his experiences in the space program. He also became a prominent public speaker, sharing his insights on space exploration and leadership.

In 1985, Collins was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, one of the highest civilian honors in the United States. He remained active in aviation and space advocacy, serving on the boards of several aerospace organizations. Collins passed away on April 28, 2021, at the age of 90, after a battle with cancer. His contributions to space exploration, particularly his role in Apollo 11, cemented his legacy as one of the key figures in the early American space program. His work in museums and diplomacy further expanded his influence beyond the spaceflight community. Collins’s life and career spanned military service, engineering, space exploration, and public leadership, making him a multifaceted figure in 20th-century history.

title: Ramli Sarip
text:
Ramli Sarip was born on November 1, 1953, in Kampung Lubok Tapang, Besut, Terengganu, Malaysia. His early life was marked by humble beginnings in a rural fishing village. His father, Sarip bin Yah, was a farmer, and his mother, Cheidin binti Ahmad, was a homemaker. Ramli was the eldest of five siblings. He received his primary education at Sekolah Kebangsaan Lubok Tapang and later attended Sekolah Menengah Kebangsaan Sultan Ismail in Besut. His academic performance was strong, particularly in mathematics and science, which later influenced his career path.

After completing his secondary education in 1971, Ramli moved to Kuala Lumpur to pursue higher studies. He enrolled at the University of Malaya, where he earned a Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering in 1975. During his university years, he was an active participant in student organizations, including the Malaysian University Engineering Society. His thesis on coastal erosion in Terengganu earned him recognition from academic circles.

Upon graduation, Ramli joined the Public Works Department (JKR) of Malaysia as a civil engineer. He worked on major infrastructure projects, including the North-South Expressway (PLUS) in the late 1980s. His expertise in structural engineering and project management quickly earned him promotions. By 1990, he was appointed as the Assistant Director of the Highway Engineering Division. His work on the PLUS project, particularly the design of the Karak Highway’s challenging terrain, was highly commended.

In 1995, Ramli was selected to lead the construction of the Sultan Mizan Zainal Abidin Stadium in Kuala Terengganu, a project that cost RM 120 million. The stadium, completed in 2002, became a landmark in Terengganu and hosted international football matches. His leadership in this project caught the attention of the Terengganu state government, and in 2003, he was appointed as the Director of the Terengganu Public Works Department.

Ramli’s career took a significant turn in 2005 when he was appointed as the Chief Executive Officer of the Malaysian Highway Authority (MHA). During his tenure, he oversaw the expansion of the federal road network, including the completion of the East Coast Expressway Phase 2 in 2015. He also played a key role in the development of the Pan Borneo Highway in Sarawak, a project spanning 1,063 kilometers. His contributions to Malaysia’s infrastructure development earned him the Federal Territory Award in 2010.

In addition to his professional achievements, Ramli was a strong advocate for engineering education. He served as a visiting lecturer at Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM) from 2008 to 2012, where he mentored over 200 engineering students. He also authored two technical manuals on highway construction, which became standard references in Malaysian engineering institutions.

Ramli retired from public service in 2018 at the age of 65. Following his retirement, he remained active in the field, consulting for private construction firms and serving on the advisory board of the Malaysian Institute of Engineers (MIE). He also dedicated time to charitable causes, particularly in his hometown of Besut, where he funded scholarships for underprivileged students.

In his later years, Ramli faced health challenges, including a diagnosis of prostate cancer in 2020. Despite treatments, his condition worsened, and he passed away on October 15, 2022, at the age of 68. He was survived by his wife, Puan Sri Rohana binti Abdul Rahim, whom he married in 1978, and their two children, a son, Mohd Fahmi, and a daughter, Nurul Huda. His funeral was held in Besut, attended by government officials, engineering colleagues, and family members.

Ramli Sarip’s legacy endures through the infrastructure projects he helped build and the students he inspired. His contributions to Malaysia’s development in engineering and public service remain widely recognized.

title: Elizabeth Inglis
text:
Elizabeth Inglis was born on May 29, 1913, in London, England, to a family with ties to the performing arts. Her father, Sir William Inglis, was a prominent British military officer, and her mother, Beatrice Frances Mary Hogg, came from a well-connected family. Elizabeth was one of four children, and her upbringing was marked by a mix of privilege and exposure to the arts. Her younger sister, Mary, also became an actress, further embedding the family in theatrical circles. Elizabeth was educated at home and later attended a finishing school in France, where she developed fluency in French.

Inglis began her acting career in the 1930s, making her stage debut in 1933 in a production of *The Constant Nymph* at the Savoy Theatre in London. Her early roles were primarily in the West End, where she gained recognition for her versatility and poise. In 1935, she made her film debut in *The Dictator*, a British comedy directed by Victor Saville. Over the next decade, she appeared in numerous films, including *The Son of Monte Cristo* (1940), *The Man Who Changed His Mind* (1936), and *A Yank at Oxford* (1938). Her performances often showcased her ability to portray elegant, sophisticated characters, a trait that became a hallmark of her career.

During World War II, Inglis continued acting but also contributed to the war effort. She performed in morale-boosting theatrical productions and supported the British war effort through public appearances and fundraisers. In 1942, she married the actor and producer George Curzon, 7th Baron Teynham. The marriage, however, was short-lived, ending in divorce in 1947. Around this time, she began a long-term relationship with the actor and writer Ronald Howard, with whom she had a son, the actor Peter Howard, born in 1945.

In the post-war years, Inglis’s career flourished. She appeared in notable films such as *The Seventh Veil* (1946), a psychological drama, and *The Winslow Boy* (1948), a courtroom drama based on a play by Terence Rattigan. Her performance in *The Seventh Veil* earned her critical acclaim, further solidifying her reputation as a serious actress. She also continued to work in theatre, starring in productions of *An Inspector Calls* (1946) and *The Heiress* (1949). Her stage work was particularly well-received, and she became one of the leading actresses of the post-war British theatre scene.

In the 1950s, Inglis transitioned to television, appearing in early British TV dramas. She starred in adaptations of classic plays and literary works, including *The Barretts of Wimpole Street* (1956) and *The Heiress* (1957). Her television work earned her a loyal following, and she became one of the first British actresses to gain significant fame on the small screen. She also continued to act in films, including *The Man Who Watched Trains Go By* (1952) and *The Heart of the Matter* (1953), though her film roles became less frequent as her television career grew.

Inglis’s later career was marked by a continued presence in theatre and television. She appeared in several BBC productions, including *The Forsyte Saga* (1967), a highly acclaimed adaptation of John Galsworthy’s novels. She also played supporting roles in films such as *The Charge of the Light Brigade* (1968) and *The Muzzle* (1971). In the 1970s, she began to take on more character roles, often portraying refined, authoritative figures, a testament to her ability to adapt to changing audiences.

By the 1980s, Inglis had largely retired from acting, though she made occasional appearances. She lived a relatively private life, dividing her time between London and the countryside. She remained close to her son, Peter Howard, who also pursued a career in acting. Inglis passed away on August 2, 1996, at the age of 83, in London. Her contributions to British theatre, film, and television were celebrated, and she left behind a legacy as one of the most respected actresses of her generation.

Throughout her career, Inglis was known for her professionalism, elegance, and dedication to her craft. She worked with some of the most prominent figures in British entertainment, including directors like Anthony Asquith and actors like Laurence Olivier. Her ability to seamlessly transition between stage, film, and television ensured her lasting influence in the industry. While she never achieved the level of mainstream fame as some of her contemporaries, her work was consistently praised for its subtlety and sophistication. Today, she is remembered as a quintessential British actress whose career spanned over six decades, leaving an indelible mark on the performing arts.

title: Don DeLillo
text:
Don DeLillo was born on November 20, 1936, in the Bronx, New York City, to Italian immigrant parents, Angelo DeLillo and Helen (née Tammaro).
